Manage documents as governed business records rather than anonymous files in a directory.

What it owns

  • Application-owned folder trees and role access.
  • File metadata, MIME information and creator details.
  • Versioned file-content records plus API and WebDAV-style exposure.

Why the boundary matters

Documents gain ownership, history and access rules that ordinary blob or filesystem storage does not provide by itself.

How it fits

The domain is published and tested independently, then composed through cCoder.Core when an application needs the complete platform. That keeps ownership visible while preserving a straightforward application bootstrap.

Getting started

The source, current README, sample hosts and tests live in cCoder.DocumentManagement on GitHub. The repository README is the version-specific starting point; the outline below explains how the pieces fit together.

Reference the package

<PackageReference Include="cCoder.DocumentManagement" Version="YOUR_VERSION" />

During coordinated local development the repositories may substitute a sibling ProjectReference. Published applications should normally consume the agreed package version so the dependency boundary remains explicit.

Register it in the host

builder.Services.AddDocumentManagementWeb(/* platform configuration */);
app.StartDocumentManagementWeb();

Configure and run it

Configure Core persistence, application ownership and the document content store. Use the HostedServices registration/startup pair when file lifecycle and event work run outside the Web process.

Consume the capability

Create application-owned folders, grant FolderRole access, then create File metadata and append versioned FileContent records. Use the document API or WebDAV-style exposure instead of bypassing governance with direct filesystem access.

Build and verify from source

git clone https://github.com/ccoder-co-uk/cCoder.DocumentManagement.git
cd cCoder.DocumentManagement
dotnet build
dotnet test

Use the repository-specific solution and test commands from its README when working on the domain itself; the standalone and acceptance-test hosts show the supported application boundary more accurately than an isolated snippet can.
